question: Which patients in a hospital setting require the use of standard precautions?

options.A: All patients regardless of their diagnosis
options.B: Patients admitted to surgical wards only
options.C: Only patients who have open wounds
options.D: Only patients with confirmed infectious diseases

explanation: Standard precautions are designed for every patient interaction because infection status is not always known upon admission. [learn more](GNS122_U2_T3#GNS122_U2_T3_h1)

question: Standard precautions apply to which of these body fluids in the ward?

options.A: Sweat from a patient exercising in physical therapy
options.B: Clean tap water used for bed baths
options.C: Saliva and wound drainage from a post-operative client
options.D: Tears collected after an eye examination

explanation: Spot on! Standard precautions cover all body fluids—except sweat. Saliva and wound drainage can carry germs, so we always protect ourselves. You are thinking like a real nurse!

question: What is the most effective single measure to prevent the spread of infections in a hospital?

options.B: Wearing sterile gloves for every task

explanation: Hand hygiene remains the single most impactful action a nurse can take to break the chain of infection. [learn more](GNS122_U2_T3#GNS122_U2_T3_h2)

question: When must a nurse choose soap and water over an alcohol-based hand rub?

options.A: When hands are visibly soiled with dirt or body fluids
options.B: Before entering a patient room for vital signs
options.C: After touching an intact patient gown

explanation: Alcohol rubs do not clean away physical dirt or certain spore-forming bacteria effectively, requiring mechanical washing with soap and water. [learn more](GNS122_U2_T3#GNS122_U2_T3_h2)

question: Which piece of PPE is primarily used to protect the nurse's clothing from splashes of body fluids?
explanation: Gowns cover the uniform and skin of the torso to block fluid splashes during high-risk procedures. [learn more](GNS122_U2_T3#GNS122_U2_T3_h3)

question: You are about to flush out a deep infected wound that might splash fluid. What PPE do you need to wear?

options.A: Sterile gloves and a gown without eye protection
options.B: Gloves, a gown, a mask, and eye protection
options.C: A mask and shoe covers only
options.D: Gloves and a surgical cap only

explanation: Brilliant! Wound splashing is unpredictable. Covering your hands, body, mouth, and eyes keeps you totally protected. Safety first!

question: What is the main reason we teach patients respiratory hygiene and cough etiquette?

options.A: Reducing the cost of cleaning medical equipment
options.C: Containing respiratory pathogens at the source
options.D: Purifying the air inside closed hospital wards

explanation: Spot on! Cough etiquette stops germs right where they start—catching them in a tissue or elbow before they can fly into the air.

question: What should a patient do right after coughing into a disposable tissue?

options.A: Place the tissue in their pocket for later use
options.B: Leave the tissue on the bedside table
options.C: Hand the tissue directly to the attending nurse
options.D: Throw the tissue in the trash and clean their hands

explanation: Correct! Tossing the tissue straight into the bin and cleaning up stops those sneaky germs from spreading to bed tables or other people.

question: What is the safest way to handle a used injection needle?

options.A: Break the needle off the syringe by hand
options.B: Drop it immediately into a puncture-resistant sharps container
options.C: Recap it firmly using both hands before walking away
options.D: Place it inside a regular plastic waste bin

explanation: You've got it! Never mess around with used needles. Drop them straight into the sharps box to avoid accidental pricks.

question: Why do we strongly advise against using both hands to recap a needle?

options.A: It damages the sharpness of the needle tip
options.B: It makes the syringe difficult to read
options.C: It greatly increases the risk of an accidental needle-stick injury
options.D: It takes too much time during an emergency

explanation: Spot on! Trying to guide a cap back on with two hands is a recipe for poking your own finger. Safety rules are written in blood—let's protect those fingers!

question: Which high-touch surface in a patient room requires frequent routine disinfection?

options.B: The inside of closed closet drawers
options.D: The ceiling tiles above the bed

explanation: High-touch items like bed rails and tables are frequently contaminated by hands and require regular cleaning. [learn more](GNS122_U2_T3#GNS122_U2_T3_h6)

question: How should a nurse handle bed sheets that are stained with blood?

options.A: Handle them with minimal agitation and bag them securely
options.B: Wash them by hand in the patient bathroom sink
options.C: Leave them on the floor until housekeeping arrives
options.D: Shake them out thoroughly to remove loose debris

explanation: You nailed it! Shaking dirty linens sends dust and germs flying everywhere. Roll them up gently and bag them safely!
